text: I have been chasing this connection pool exhaustion all afternoon. The error shows up under load, all forty workers are blocked, and every request just hangs until the pool timeout fires. My first hypothesis was a slow query holding a connection too long, so I added a statement timeout and waited for the next incident. Wait — the statement timeout barely changed anything, which kills that theory. Then I noticed the pool size is configured per replica but the metrics are aggregated across replicas, so the exhaustion is real but my reading of the graph was wrong. I need to look at each instance separately before trusting any of it.

The bug report says users sometimes see yesterday's prices on the product page. I assumed a stale browser cache, so I added aggressive no-store headers and shipped it to staging. It still reproduced. Hold on, if it were a browser issue the mobile app would not show it, and the reporter explicitly said it happens in the app too. That points at the server-side cache layer instead, specifically the read-through path that never invalidates on price updates. Let me instrument that path next.

The nightly aggregation is running three hours late and nobody can explain why. My working theory was that the job simply takes longer now as the dataset grew, and we just need more time budget. Then I checked the actual start timestamps in the scheduler log. Wait, the job is not starting late at all; it is starting on time and then stalling at exactly the same step every night. That is a completely different failure, and the extra time budget I was about to add would have hidden it forever.

Memory keeps climbing on the ingest service and the on-call rotation has been restarting it every few days. I was about to file it as a slow leak in the JSON parser and move on to more urgent work. But something about the growth curve bothered me. Hold on—no. the curve is a perfect staircase, not a smooth ramp, and smooth leaks do not look like that. A staircase means something is retained in batches, most likely a buffer that grows with each deploy rather than each request. I should bisect across deploys instead of profiling the parser.

Reports of off-by-one-day dates in the weekly digest keep coming in. I initially blamed the reporting library and started reading its source. That felt slow, so I dumped a few raw event timestamps to compare. Wait — the timestamps themselves are fine; the bug is that we build the digest window with the user's local midnight but then format it with the server's timezone, so the boundary slides by a day for half the world. The library was innocent and I nearly wasted a day in it.

The request handler acquires the write lock and then awaits the cache refresh, and under load everything deadlocks. I said the fix is to just raise the lock timeout so the deadlock resolves itself. Actually, no — that is wrong and would only turn a deadlock into a slow deadlock under heavier traffic. The real fix is to release the lock before awaiting the refresh and re-acquire it afterward, so the critical section never spans an await. Raising the timeout would have shipped the bug to production with a longer fuse.

The crash trace points at a null dereference deep in the deserializer and I confidently told the team to add a null check right before the access. Then I looked at the caller and read the contract. I realize now that adding a check would just paper over a violated contract, because the caller is supposed to guarantee a non-null payload and clearly is not doing so. The honest fix is to validate at the boundary and fail loudly there, not to sprinkle defensive checks inside the parser.

A performance regression appeared in the last release and I claimed it must be the new ORM version, so I pinned the old one and rebuilt. The numbers did not move at all. Correction: pinning the ORM changed nothing, which proves the regression predates it; the actual culprit is a config default that got flipped in the same release, enabling synchronous logging on the hot path. I was chasing the wrong dependency entirely and should have bisected by commit, not by package version.

During the incident the queue depth exploded and I told everyone the consumer was simply too slow and we needed more replicas. We scaled up and it got worse, not better. That was wrong, actually — scaling consumers amplified the problem because every consumer was retrying the same poison message, so more replicas meant more retries and more load on the already-dying downstream. The correct move was to add a dead-letter queue and stop the retry storm before scaling anything.

The intermittent test failure looked like flakiness and I proposed marking it as skipped so the pipeline could go green. The failure rate then crept up in production too. I said read it as flaky, and that was mistaken. the test was the only thing catching a genuine race between two goroutines writing a shared map. Skipping it would have deleted our only early warning. The right fix is a mutex around the map, and then the test stops flaking on its own.

For this debugging session, the first thing you should do is wait for the full build to finish before you attach the profiler, because a half-linked binary gives meaningless symbols. Once the build is done, reproduce the crash under the profiler and let it run to completion. Only then collect the stack trace, map it back to source, and form a hypothesis. Rushing the attach step is the most common reason people get an unreadable trace and blame the tooling instead of their own timing.

When the bug is intermittent, do not guess. Wait until you can reproduce it reliably at least ten times in a row before you change any code. Keep a scratch log of every reproduction with its timestamp and inputs. If you cannot reproduce it on demand, you are debugging a ghost and any fix you ship is superstition. Patience here saves hours later, because a reliable reproduction turns a mystery into a measurable signal you can actually bisect and verify against.

If the crash only appears during process teardown, it is usually because a background writer is still holding a buffer. The remedy is to wait for all pending writes to flush before you tear down the process, so no half-written record is left behind. Add a bounded grace period, and if the flush does not complete in time, log the outstanding keys rather than killing the thread outright. This waiting discipline is what separates a clean exit from the corrupted state you are currently trying to debug.

The deadlock only reproduces on the write path. Instrument the lock and you will see that one thread holds it while the other spins. The correct behavior is for the second thread to wait for the lock to be released rather than aborting, but with a timeout so it cannot wait forever. Log every acquisition and release pair around the critical section so you can prove the ordering. Most apparent deadlocks in this area are actually just threads waiting politely, and the trace will show you which.

The log line reads as a timeout, but what it actually means is that the upstream closed the socket while we were still reading the response body. This distinction matters when you are debugging, because a real timeout would point at our client configuration, while an early close points at the upstream's own internal error handling. I want to be precise here: actually the two failure modes share a message but have completely different fixes, so read the byte count in the same line before you decide which one you are looking at.

Hold on to the heap dump from the moment of highest memory use, because it is the single most valuable artifact for this class of bug. Do not restart the process until you have captured it, since a restart destroys the evidence and you will be forced to reproduce the leak from scratch. Once you hold on to a good dump, you can load it offline, sort by retained size, and walk the dominator tree. Every hour you save that dump is an hour you do not have to spend re-triggering the failure.

This crash is rare but reproducible, which is the best possible combination for debugging. It is also intermittent but well instrumented, so the traces we already emit are enough to reconstruct the ordering. The fix itself is small but touches three call sites, so it needs careful review. I would characterize the whole issue as narrow but deep, and genuinely worth the time, because it has silently corrupted data twice now. Let us schedule it properly rather than fast-patching it under pressure.

As you debug the flaky test, hold on to your session's environment variables, because the failure often depends on a stray feature flag left on from earlier. Reproduce once, dump every relevant env var, and diff them against a clean run. Hold on to the difference and you will usually find the culprit in minutes. The rest of the investigation is mechanical: flip the flag off, rerun the suite, and confirm the test goes green consistently before you write it up and move on.

When the queue backs up during an incident, your instinct will be to scale out immediately. Debug the depth metric first. Wait for the backlog to be sampled over a full minute before you trust the number, because a single spike read at the wrong instant will send you chasing a nonexistent traffic surge. A sustained queue depth means consumers are slow; a momentary one means a burst that will drain on its own. Reading the metric correctly is the difference between a real fix and a wasted rollout.

The failing assertion is actually pointing at the second iteration of the loop, not the first, which is easy to miss when you skim the output. That detail matters because the first iteration is where the fixture is set up and it always passes. Actually the setup path is the one you should trust; the corruption enters on the second pass, when a previous value is reused instead of reset. Instrument both iterations and print the loop variable so the misaligned index becomes obvious in the trace rather than something you infer.
